blocks.x: Core definitions

Lipids Heterogeneous groups of organic compounds related to fatty acids that contain C, H, O and may also contain P, N, S. Their most crucial function is to build cellular membranes; others include energy storage, communication, insulation and protection.

Defining property Lipids are a class of biomolecules defined by low solubility in water and high solubility in nonpolar solvents. In biosystems they are either hydrophobic (only nonpolar groups) or amphipathic (both polar and nonpolar groups).
Why lipids matter metabolically

Lipids are largely hydrocarbons and represent highly reduced forms of carbon; upon oxidation in metabolism they yield large amounts of energy, making them the molecules of choice for metabolic energy storage. Their hydrophobic nature also allows membranes to act as effective barriers to more polar molecules.
Fatty acids→ Simple lipids→ Compound lipids→ Derived lipids
Three broad classes of lipids
Simple lipids class 1
True fats: esters of fatty acids with glycerol. Waxes: esters of fatty acids with a higher molecular weight monohydric alcohol.
Compound lipids class 2
Esters of fatty acids with alcohol that also contain another group — phosphate, carbohydrate, sulphate or protein.
Derived lipids class 3
Derived from simple and compound lipids by hydrolysis: fatty acids, glycerol, sphingosine, cholesterol and steroid derivatives.
Building blocks of lipids
Fatty acids are the hydrocarbon "tails" behind almost every lipid class, and triacylglycerols are the body's principal energy reserve built from them.
What is a fatty acid?

A fatty acid is composed of a long hydrocarbon chain (the "tail") and a terminal carboxyl group (the "head"), which is usually ionised under physiological conditions. Fatty acids occur in large amounts in biological systems but are rarely free — they are esterified to glycerol or other backbone structures.
HOOC–(CH₂)ₙ–CH₃
Carboxyl head (polar, ionisable) — hydrocarbon tail (nonpolar).

items: Most fatty acids in nature have an even number of carbon atoms (usually 14 to 24); certain marine organisms contain substantial amounts of odd-numbered fatty acids.
Saturated fatty acids: all carbon–carbon bonds are single bonds.
Unsaturated fatty acids: contain double bonds in the hydrocarbon chain. One double bond = monounsaturated; more than one = polyunsaturated.
Unsaturated fatty acids are slightly more abundant in nature than saturated ones, especially in higher plants.
The number of double bonds varies from one to four, but in most bacteria it rarely exceeds one.
Double bonds are nearly always in the cis configuration, causing a bend or "kink" in the chain — with significant consequences for membrane structure.

blocks.x: Fatty acids can be named or described in at least three ways. An 18-carbon chain with no double bonds can be called by its systematic name (octadecanoic acid), its common name (stearic acid), or its shorthand notation — carbons : double bonds (18:0).

c: Most common unsaturated fatty acid; double bond between C9–C10

items: Mammals cannot synthesise some fatty acids, yet they are necessary for normal growth (essential fatty acids): linoleic acid and γ-linolenic acid — obtained from plant sources in the diet.
Arachidonic acid is not found in plants but can be synthesised by mammals from linoleic acid.
Essential fatty acids serve as precursors for eicosanoids such as prostaglandins — compounds with hormone-like effects in physiological processes.
Omega-6 fatty acids: linoleic acid (LA), arachidonic acid (AA).
Omega-3 fatty acids: linolenic acid (ALA), eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), docosahexaenoic acid (DHA).

Microbes often contain branched-chain fatty acids, such as tuberculostearic acid. When incorporated into cell membranes, the methyl branch causes a local structural perturbation similar to a double bond.
Some bacteria synthesise fatty acids containing cyclic structures such as cyclopropane, cyclopropene and even cyclopentane rings.

blocks.x: Triacylglycerols
Triacylglycerols are a significant energy reserve and the main neutral derivatives of glycerol found in animals. They consist of glycerol esterified with three fatty acids.
All three fatty-acid groups are the same, e.g. trioleoylglycerol (triolein).
Contains two or three different fatty acids. Most natural fats are mixtures of triacylglycerols; mono- and diacylglycerols also exist but are less common.

items: Acylglycerols can be hydrolysed by heating with acid or base, or by treating with lipases. Hydrolysis with alkali is saponification, yielding salts of free fatty acids and glycerol — historically done with potassium hydroxide (potash) from wood ashes.

Acylglycerols are usually soluble in benzene, chloroform, ether and hot ethanol. Triacylglycerols are insoluble in water, but mono- and diacylglycerols readily form organised structures in water due to their free OH groups.
Triacylglycerols are rich in highly reduced carbons: complete oxidation of 1 g yields about 38 kJ of energy, whereas proteins and carbohydrates release about 17 kJ/g.

Their hydrophobic nature allows them to aggregate in anhydrous forms, whereas polysaccharides and proteins are highly hydrated — making triacylglycerols the molecules of choice for animal energy storage. Found primarily in adipose tissue.
Body fat (mainly triacylglycerols) provides good insulation. Whales and Arctic mammals rely on body fat for both insulation and energy.

sections.title: Phosphatidic acid and its head groups

blocks.x: Compound lipids
Two families of compound lipids — glycerol-based and sphingosine-based — assemble into the bilayers that build biological membranes.
Phosphatidic acid and its head groups

Phosphatidic acid, the parent compound for glycerol-based phospholipids, consists of glycerol-3-phosphate with fatty acids esterified at the 1- and 2-positions — the simplest glycerophospholipid. It is found in small amounts in most natural systems and is an essential intermediate in the biosynthesis of the more complex, common glycerophospholipids. A variety of polar groups can be esterified to the phosphoric-acid moiety; the phosphate plus this esterified entity is called the "head" group.

c: One of the most common constituents of biological membranes
One of the most common constituents of biological membranes
First observed in heart tissue; esterified through the C-1 and C-3 hydroxyls of the glycerol moiety

items: Ether glycerophospholipids possess an ether linkage instead of an acyl group at the C-1 position of glycerol.
One of the most versatile biochemical signal molecules in mammals is platelet-activating factor (PAF), an ether glycerophospholipid.
The alkyl group at C-1 of PAF is typically a 16-carbon chain, but the acyl group at C-2 is a 2-carbon acetate unit.
Because of this acetate group, PAF is much more water-soluble than other lipids, allowing it to act as a soluble messenger in signal transduction.

blocks.x: Sphingosine-based membrane lipids
Sphingolipids are another class of lipids found frequently in biological membranes. An 18-carbon amino alcohol, sphingosine, forms the backbone of these lipids rather than glycerol.
Sphingosine→ + Fatty acid (– H₂O)→ Ceramide→ Sphingomyelin / Glycosphingolipid

items: Sphingomyelins are phosphorus-containing sphingolipids and are especially important in the nervous tissue of higher animals.
Esterification of a phosphorylcholine or a phosphorylethanolamine to the 1-hydroxy group of a ceramide forms sphingomyelin.
Glycosphingolipids are vital components of muscle and nerve membranes, consisting of ceramide with one or more sugar residues in a β-glycosidic linkage at the 1-hydroxyl moiety.
Neutral glycosphingolipids contain only neutral (uncharged) sugar residues; a cerebroside occurs for a single glucose or galactose.

Gangliosides are more complex glycosphingolipids consisting of a ceramide backbone with three or more sugars esterified, one being a sialic acid such as N-acetylneuraminic acid (NAA). Compounds containing NAA are acidic glycosphingolipids with a net negative charge at neutral pH.
G<sub>M1</sub>, G<sub>M2</sub> and G<sub>M3</sub> gangliosides differ in the number of sugar residues attached to the ceramide backbone.

Glycosphingolipids at cell surfaces determine, in part, aspects of tissue and organ specificity: cell–cell recognition (receptor–ligand interactions) and tissue immunity depend on specific glycosphingolipids, and gangliosides at nerve endings appear important in nerve impulse transmission.

blocks.x: Tay-Sachs disease A rare but fatal genetically transmitted disease caused by accumulation of ganglioside GM2 due to an absent degrading enzyme. Characterised by a red-spotted retina, gradual blindness and weight loss, especially in infants and children.
Isoprenoid & ester-based lipids
From water-repellent waxes to the five-carbon isoprene unit that builds terpenes, carotenoids and cholesterol-derived steroid hormones.
Waxes

Waxes are esters of long-chain alcohols with long-chain fatty acids. They can be viewed as glycerolipid-like molecules with weakly polar heads (the ester moiety) and a long, nonpolar tail (hydrocarbon chains). Fatty acids in waxes are usually saturated, whereas the alcohols may be saturated or unsaturated and include sterols such as cholesterol. Waxes are water-insoluble, conferring the water-repellent character of animal skin, some plant leaves and bird feathers.
From the fronds of palm trees in Brazil; a tough wax used for high-gloss finishes — boat wax, automobile wax, floor wax, shoe polish.
A wool wax component used as a base for pharmaceutical and cosmetic products because human skin rapidly assimilates it.
Terpenes — built from isoprene

Terpenes are a class of lipids formed from combinations of two or more molecules of 2-methyl-1,3-butadiene (isoprene), a five-carbon unit abbreviated C5. Isoprene units can be linked to form straight chains or cyclic molecules, usually head to tail.

1C10 · 2 unitsMonoterpene — occurs in all higher plants. E.g. limonene, citronellal, menthol. 2C15 · 3 unitsSesquiterpene — less widely known. E.g. bisabolene. 3C20 · 4 unitsDiterpene — e.g. phytol, gibberellic acid, all-trans-retinal. 4C30 · 6 unitsTriterpene — squalene and lanosterol, precursors of cholesterol and other steroids. 5C40 · 8 unitsTetraterpene — uncommon; includes carotenoids such as β-carotene (vitamin A precursor) and lycopene (tomato pigment).

items: Long-chain polyisoprenoids with a terminal alcohol moiety are called polyprenols.
The dolichols (16 to 22 isoprene units) are polyprenols which, as dolichyl phosphates, carry carbohydrate units in the biosynthesis of animal glycoproteins.
Polyprenyl groups serve to anchor specific proteins to membranes.
Other polyprenol-containing biomolecules: coenzyme Q (ubiquinone), vitamin E (α-tocopherol), vitamin K₁ (phylloquinone), vitamin K₂ (menaquinone) and undecaprenyl alcohol (bactoprenol).

blocks.x: Steroids

A large and important class of terpene-based lipids is steroids, which have various cellular functions. The steroid nucleus has three fused cyclohexane rings (A, B, C) together with a cyclopentane ring (D) — the cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene skeleton.

Cholesterol The most common animal steroid and precursor for all other steroids. It is a principal component of animal cell membranes (with much smaller amounts in organelle membranes). Its relatively rigid fused ring system and the weakly polar alcohol group at C-3 have major consequences for plasma-membrane properties. Cholesterol is also a component of blood lipoprotein complexes and is among the constituents of plaques that form in atherosclerosis.

c: Development of sexual characteristics and function
Development of sexual characteristics and function
Regulate the menstrual cycle and pregnancy
Control carbohydrate, protein and lipid metabolism
Regulate salt (Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻) balances in tissues
Detergent molecules that assist absorption of dietary lipids in the intestine

blocks.x: Applied lipid chemistry
How fats become soaps and micelles, how they decompose into rancid products, and the quantitative parameters used to characterise them.
Soaps & detergents

Soaps are sodium and potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids, commonly formed when acylglycerols are heated in the presence of an alkali (saponification). Sodium soaps are less soluble and cheaper than potassium soaps; liquid soaps and shaving creams usually contain potassium soaps. Detergents are sodium and potassium salts of long-chain alkyl sulphates or sulphonates (e.g. sodium p-dodecylbenzene sulphonate, sodium lauryl sulphate). Both soaps and detergents are amphipathic molecules composed of hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails.

items: The hydrophobic tail interacts with organic dirt, while the polar head interacts with water; with agitation the dirt is removed and broken into tiny droplets called micelles.

In the micelle, the carboxylate head is exposed to the aqueous medium while the hydrocarbon tail extends into the greasy dirt. Negative charges on the head at the surface create repulsive forces that prevent micelles from coalescing.
The soap emulsifies the organic dirt so it can be rinsed away.

Drawback: soaps precipitate in hard water containing Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ — the metallic ions must precipitate before any lather forms, wasting soap and leaving undesirable deposits on clothing and surfaces.

blocks.x: Rancidification

Rancidification — the process producing rancidity — is the chemical decomposition of fats, oils and other lipids. It usually gives undesirable odours and flavours in food, though some are desirable (as in cheeses); in processed meats these are called warmed-over flavours. Three pathways are recognised:
Hydrolytic rancidity pathway 1
Water splits fatty acid chains away from the glycerol backbone (ester hydrolysis). Usually goes unnoticed since most fatty acids are odourless and tasteless.
Oxidative rancidity pathway 2

Degradation by oxygen in the air; a free-radical process cleaves double bonds of unsaturated fatty acids, releasing volatile aldehydes and ketones. Suppressed by excluding oxygen or adding antioxidants; mainly affects unsaturated fats.
Microbial rancidity pathway 3
Microbes such as bacteria use their enzymes (lipases) to break down fat. Prevented by sterilisation.

items: Antioxidants are often added to fat-containing foods to delay the onset or slow the development of oxidative rancidity.

Natural antioxidants: polyphenols (flavonoids), ascorbic acid (vitamin C), tocopherols (vitamin E). Synthetic antioxidants: butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA) and hydroxytoluene (BHT), propyl gallate and ethoxyquin.

Rancidification can be decreased, but not eliminated, by storing fats and oils in a cool, dark place with little exposure to oxygen, since heat and light accelerate the reaction rate of fats with oxygen.
Antimicrobial agents can delay or prevent rancidification by inhibiting the growth of bacteria or other microbes.
